title: Advanced Diffusion Models (ControlNet, LoRA)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Advanced Diffusion Models (ControlNet, LoRA) ##### The catalogue that needed the same chair 40 times A furniture retailer in Jaipur wanted lifestyle imagery for their catalogue — each product shown in a styled room, from consistent angles, across four seasonal themes. 160 images. Their designer tried plain Stable Diffusion prompting for two weeks. Every generation produced a beautiful room containing a chair that was **not their chair**. Different proportions, different upholstery pattern, different leg profile. Prompt engineering could not fix it, because the model had never seen their product and text cannot specify a physical object precisely enough. The fix was two techniques used together. A **DreamBooth LoRA** trained on 22 photographs of the actual chair taught the model that specific object. **ControlNet** conditioned on a depth map from a reference photo locked the camera angle and composition. 160 images in three days, each showing their real chair in a controlled pose. **Day 38 of the beginner track covered prompting diffusion models. That gets you variety, not control.** Today is the techniques that make generation specifiable — which is the difference between a toy and a production pipeline. ##### Latent diffusion internals The three components, and what each does. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph TRAIN["Training"] A["Image 512×512×3"] --> B["VAE encoder"] B --> C["Latent 64×64×4"] C --> D["+ noise at timestep t"] D --> E["U-Net predicts noise"] F["Text prompt"] --> G["CLIP text encoder"] G -.cross-attention.-> E E --> H["MSE loss vs actual noise"] end subgraph INFER["Inference"] I["Random latent 64×64×4"] --> J["U-Net denoise × N steps"] K["Prompt embedding"] -.cross-attention.-> J J --> L["Clean latent"] L --> M["VAE decoder"] M --> N["Image 512×512×3"] end ``` **The VAE** compresses 512×512×3 = 786,432 values into 64×64×4 = 16,384 — a 48× reduction. Diffusion runs entirely in that space, which is why Stable Diffusion fits on consumer hardware. **The U-Net** is where everything interesting happens. It is a convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections, and — critically — **cross-attention layers at multiple resolutions** where the text embedding enters. ```python import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLPipeline, UNet2DConditionModel pipe = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0", torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant="fp16", ).to("cuda") unet = pipe.unet print(f"U-Net parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in unet.parameters())/1e6:.0f}M") # The cross-attention layers are where ControlNet and LoRA hook in attn_names = [n for n, _ in unet.named_modules() if "attn2" in n] print(f"cross-attention blocks: {len(attn_names)}") ``` **Cross-attention resolution determines what the text controls.** Low-resolution blocks (8×8, 16×16) govern composition and layout; high-resolution blocks (64×64) govern texture and fine detail. This is why prompt weighting affects different aspects unpredictably — you are influencing all of them at once. **SDXL versus SD 1.5**, which matters for practical choices: | | SD 1.5 | SDXL | |---|---|---| | Native resolution | 512×512 | **1024×1024** | | U-Net parameters | 860M | **2.6B** | | Text encoders | CLIP ViT-L | **CLIP ViT-L + OpenCLIP ViT-bigG** | | Latent channels | 4 | 4 | | VRAM (inference) | ~4 GB | ~10 GB | | Ecosystem (LoRAs, ControlNets) | **Largest** | Large and growing | | Prompt adherence | Moderate | **Better** | **SD 1.5 still has the deeper ecosystem** of community LoRAs and ControlNets, and it is far cheaper to train on. SDXL produces better images and follows prompts more closely. For a production pipeline in 2026, SDXL unless VRAM or training budget forces otherwise. ##### Samplers and schedulers The sampler decides how to step from noise to image, and the choice affects both quality and speed substantially. ```python from diffusers import (DPMSolverMultistepScheduler, EulerDiscreteScheduler, EulerAncestralDiscreteScheduler, DDIMScheduler, UniPCMultistepScheduler, LCMScheduler) SCHEDULERS = { "DPM++ 2M Karras": lambda cfg: DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config( cfg, use_karras_sigmas=True, algorithm_type="dpmsolver++"), "DPM++ SDE Karras": lambda cfg: DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config( cfg, use_karras_sigmas=True, algorithm_type="sde-dpmsolver++"), "Euler": lambda cfg: EulerDiscreteScheduler.from_config(cfg), "Euler a": lambda cfg: EulerAncestralDiscreteScheduler.from_config(cfg), "UniPC": lambda cfg: UniPCMultistepScheduler.from_config(cfg), "DDIM": lambda cfg: DDIMScheduler.from_config(cfg), } pipe.scheduler = SCHEDULERS["DPM++ 2M Karras"](pipe.scheduler.config) ``` | Sampler | Steps for good quality | Deterministic | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | **DPM++ 2M Karras** | **20–30** | Yes | **The default recommendation** | | DPM++ SDE Karras | 25–35 | No | More detail, less reproducible | | Euler | 25–40 | Yes | Simple, reliable | | Euler a | 20–30 | **No** | Ancestral — never fully converges | | UniPC | 15–25 | Yes | Fastest convergence | | DDIM | 40–50 | Yes | Older; supports inversion | | LCM | **4–8** | Yes | Needs an LCM-LoRA; real-time capable | **Ancestral samplers (the `a` suffix) inject fresh noise at each step**, so the image keeps changing as you add steps rather than converging. That makes them poor for reproducible pipelines but useful when exploring variety. **Karras sigma scheduling** redistributes noise levels to spend more steps where they matter. It is essentially free quality and should be on by default. **LCM and Turbo variants** are distilled models that generate in 4–8 steps. Quality is below full-step generation, but at roughly 200ms per image they enable interactive workflows. ```python def benchmark_samplers(pipe, prompt, seed=42, steps_list=(10, 20, 30, 50)): """Quality plateaus at different points for different samplers.""" import time results = [] for name, factory in SCHEDULERS.items(): pipe.scheduler = factory(pipe.scheduler.config) for steps in steps_list: g = torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(seed) t0 = time.perf_counter() image = pipe(prompt, num_inference_steps=steps, guidance_scale=7.0, generator=g).images[0] results.append({"sampler": name, "steps": steps, "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2)}) image.save(f"bench_{name.replace(' ', '_')}_{steps}.png") return results ``` ##### ControlNet The technique that gives you structural control. Zhang et al. (2023) add a trainable copy of the U-Net encoder that takes a conditioning image and injects features into the frozen base U-Net through **zero-initialised convolutions**. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Conditioning image
depth / pose / edges"] --> B["ControlNet
trainable copy of
U-Net encoder"] B --> C["Zero conv layers
output 0 at init"] D["Noisy latent"] --> E["Frozen U-Net"] C -->|"added to skip
connections"| E F["Text prompt"] -.cross-attention.-> E E --> G["Denoised latent"] H["Zero init means training
starts as the unmodified model"] -.-> C ``` **Zero-initialised convolutions are the same idea as LoRA's zero-initialised B matrix** (Day 12) — at step zero the ControlNet contributes nothing, so training starts from the base model's behaviour rather than a random perturbation of it. ```python import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLControlNetPipeline, ControlNetModel from controlnet_aux import (CannyDetector, MidasDetector, OpenposeDetector, LineartDetector) from PIL import Image controlnet = ControlNetModel.from_pretrained( "diffusers/controlnet-depth-sdxl-1.0", torch_dtype=torch.float16) pipe = StableDiffusionXLControlNetPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0", controlnet=controlnet, torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant="fp16", ).to("cuda") pipe.enable_model_cpu_offload() depth_estimator = MidasDetector.from_pretrained("lllyasviel/Annotators") reference = Image.open("reference_room.jpg").convert("RGB").resize((1024, 1024)) depth_map = depth_estimator(reference) image = pipe( prompt=("editorial interior photograph, Jaipur haveli living room, " "terracotta walls, jharokha window, warm afternoon light, " "35mm lens, shallow depth of field"), negative_prompt="blurry, distorted, watermark, text, lowres, oversaturated", image=depth_map, controlnet_conditioning_scale=0.7, control_guidance_start=0.0, control_guidance_end=0.8, num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=6.5, generator=torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(42), ).images[0] ``` **The three ControlNet parameters, and what they actually do:** - **`controlnet_conditioning_scale`** (0.0–2.0) — how strongly the condition binds. Below 0.5 it is a suggestion; above 1.2 it dominates and quality degrades. **0.6–0.9 is the working range.** - **`control_guidance_start`** — when conditioning begins. Leave at 0.0. - **`control_guidance_end`** — when it stops. **Setting this to 0.7–0.85 is the technique people miss**: release the condition for the final steps so the model can refine texture and lighting freely while composition stays locked. **The ControlNet types, and when each is right:** | Type | Conditioning input | Controls | Use for | |---|---|---|---| | **Depth** | Depth map (MiDaS) | 3D layout, camera angle | **Product photography, interiors** | | **Canny** | Edge map | Exact outlines | Preserving precise shapes, logos | | **OpenPose** | Skeleton keypoints | Human pose | Fashion, character work | | **Lineart** | Clean line drawing | Illustration structure | Concept art, colouring sketches | | **Scribble** | Rough sketch | Loose composition | Ideation from a hand drawing | | **Segmentation** | Semantic mask | Region-wise content | Architectural, scene layout | | **Tile** | Downscaled image | Detail at high resolution | Upscaling, detail enhancement | | **Normal** | Surface normals | Lighting and surface | 3D-aware relighting | **Depth is the most generally useful** for product and interior work — it preserves spatial relationships and camera perspective without over-constraining surface detail the way Canny does. **Multi-ControlNet** composes several conditions: ```python from diffusers import ControlNetModel controlnets = [ ControlNetModel.from_pretrained("diffusers/controlnet-depth-sdxl-1.0", torch_dtype=torch.float16), ControlNetModel.from_pretrained("diffusers/controlnet-canny-sdxl-1.0", torch_dtype=torch.float16), ] pipe = StableDiffusionXLControlNetPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0", controlnet=controlnets, torch_dtype=torch.float16).to("cuda") image = pipe( prompt=prompt, image=[depth_map, canny_map], controlnet_conditioning_scale=[0.6, 0.35], # depth dominant, canny light num_inference_steps=30, ).images[0] ``` **Keep the combined scales under about 1.2.** Two ControlNets at 0.8 each over-constrain the generation and produce rigid, artefact-heavy output. ##### LoRA for diffusion Same low-rank idea as Day 12, applied to the U-Net's cross-attention layers. ```python from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLPipeline import torch pipe = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0", torch_dtype=torch.float16).to("cuda") # Load and weight multiple LoRAs pipe.load_lora_weights("./loras/jaipur-chair", adapter_name="product") pipe.load_lora_weights("./loras/editorial-style", adapter_name="style") pipe.set_adapters(["product", "style"], adapter_weights=[0.9, 0.5]) image = pipe( prompt="photo of sks chair in a sunlit Jaipur courtyard, editorial style", num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=6.5, ).images[0] pipe.unload_lora_weights() # clean up between different combinations ``` **Adapter weights are the practical control.** A subject LoRA at 0.9 and a style LoRA at 0.5 lets the product dominate while the style tints. Both at 1.0 usually produces conflict artefacts. ##### Training a subject LoRA with DreamBooth The Jaipur chair. DreamBooth (Ruiz et al., 2022) teaches a specific subject by binding it to a rare token. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class DreamBoothConfig: instance_prompt: str = "a photo of sks chair" class_prompt: str = "a photo of chair" instance_images: int = 22 class_images: int = 200 # prior preservation resolution: int = 1024 rank: int = 32 learning_rate: float = 1e-4 text_encoder_lr: float = 5e-5 max_train_steps: int = 1200 train_text_encoder: bool = True prior_loss_weight: float = 1.0 ``` ```bash accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_sdxl.py \ --pretrained_model_name_or_path="stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0" \ --pretrained_vae_model_name_or_path="madebyollin/sdxl-vae-fp16-fix" \ --instance_data_dir="./data/chair" \ --class_data_dir="./data/class_chair" \ --output_dir="./loras/jaipur-chair" \ --instance_prompt="a photo of sks chair" \ --class_prompt="a photo of chair" \ --with_prior_preservation --prior_loss_weight=1.0 \ --num_class_images=200 \ --resolution=1024 --train_batch_size=1 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps=4 --gradient_checkpointing \ --learning_rate=1e-4 --text_encoder_lr=5e-5 --train_text_encoder \ --lr_scheduler="constant_with_warmup" --lr_warmup_steps=100 \ --rank=32 --max_train_steps=1200 \ --mixed_precision="fp16" --use_8bit_adam \ --validation_prompt="a photo of sks chair in a garden" \ --validation_epochs=50 --seed=42 ``` **Prior preservation is what prevents language drift.** Without it, fine-tuning on 22 chair photos causes the model to associate the word "chair" itself with your specific chair — every chair it generates becomes yours. Generating 200 class images of generic chairs and training on both keeps the general concept intact. **The rare token matters.** `sks` is conventional because it has almost no prior meaning in CLIP's vocabulary. Using a real word like `jaipurchair` inherits whatever associations those subword tokens already carry. **Training data guidance for a subject LoRA:** | Aspect | Recommendation | |---|---| | Image count | 15–30 (more is not better) | | Backgrounds | **Varied** — otherwise the background is learned too | | Angles | 5+ distinct viewpoints | | Lighting | 3+ conditions | | Resolution | At or above training resolution | | Cropping | Subject fills 50–80% of the frame | | Captions | Consistent instance prompt; avoid over-describing | **Varied backgrounds is the rule people break.** Twenty photos of the chair in the same studio produces a LoRA that generates the chair *and that studio*, inseparably. **Steps and overfitting:** ```python def dreambooth_step_guidance(n_images: int, rank: int = 32, train_text_encoder: bool = True) -> dict: base = n_images * 50 # ~50 steps per image if rank > 32: base = int(base * 0.8) if train_text_encoder: base = int(base * 0.9) return {"recommended_steps": base, "check_at": [int(base * 0.5), int(base * 0.75), base], "note": "Save checkpoints and compare — overfitting shows as " "the subject appearing in every generation regardless " "of the prompt, and loss of pose flexibility."} ``` **Save intermediate checkpoints and compare them.** Overfitting in DreamBooth is visually obvious once you look — the subject stops responding to pose and context instructions — and the best checkpoint is frequently not the last. **Style LoRAs differ from subject LoRAs:** | | Subject LoRA | Style LoRA | |---|---|---| | Images | 15–30 of one thing | 50–200 in one style | | Trigger token | Rare token (`sks`) | Style name | | Prior preservation | **Essential** | Usually unnecessary | | Rank | 16–32 | 8–16 | | Steps | 1,000–1,500 | 2,000–4,000 | | Text encoder | Train it | Often skip | ##### IP-Adapter The lighter-weight alternative to training: condition on a *reference image* rather than a trained LoRA. ```python from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLPipeline from transformers import CLIPVisionModelWithProjection import torch image_encoder = CLIPVisionModelWithProjection.from_pretrained( "h94/IP-Adapter", subfolder="sdxl_models/image_encoder", torch_dtype=torch.float16) pipe = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0", image_encoder=image_encoder, torch_dtype=torch.float16).to("cuda") pipe.load_ip_adapter("h94/IP-Adapter", subfolder="sdxl_models", weight_name="ip-adapter-plus_sdxl_vit-h.safetensors") pipe.set_ip_adapter_scale(0.6) reference = Image.open("style_reference.jpg") image = pipe( prompt="a Jaipur courtyard at golden hour", ip_adapter_image=reference, num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=6.0, ).images[0] ``` **IP-Adapter injects CLIP image embeddings through additional cross-attention layers** — effectively "a prompt, but an image." No training required, immediate results. **When to use which:** | Need | Technique | Training | |---|---|---| | A specific object, high fidelity | **DreamBooth LoRA** | 20–40 min | | A consistent style across many images | **Style LoRA** | 1–2 hours | | Style transfer from one reference | **IP-Adapter** | **None** | | Face consistency | IP-Adapter FaceID / InstantID | None | | Exact composition or pose | **ControlNet** | None | | Object + composition | **LoRA + ControlNet** | LoRA only | **IP-Adapter is the right first attempt** because it costs nothing to try. Reach for a LoRA when you need higher fidelity to a specific subject than a reference image can convey. ##### The production pipeline Combining everything, as the Jaipur team did. ```python import torch from dataclasses import dataclass from diffusers import (StableDiffusionXLControlNetPipeline, ControlNetModel, DPMSolverMultistepScheduler, AutoencoderKL) from controlnet_aux import MidasDetector from PIL import Image @dataclass class GenerationSpec: prompt: str negative_prompt: str = ("blurry, distorted, deformed, watermark, text, " "lowres, jpeg artifacts, oversaturated, extra limbs") reference_image: str = None control_scale: float = 0.7 control_end: float = 0.8 lora_weights: dict = None # {adapter_name: weight} steps: int = 30 guidance: float = 6.5 seed: int = None width: int = 1024 height: int = 1024 class ControlledGenerator: def __init__(self, base_model="stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0"): vae = AutoencoderKL.from_pretrained("madebyollin/sdxl-vae-fp16-fix", torch_dtype=torch.float16) controlnet = ControlNetModel.from_pretrained( "diffusers/controlnet-depth-sdxl-1.0", torch_dtype=torch.float16) self.pipe = StableDiffusionXLControlNetPipeline.from_pretrained( base_model, controlnet=controlnet, vae=vae, torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant="fp16") self.pipe.scheduler = DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config( self.pipe.scheduler.config, use_karras_sigmas=True, algorithm_type="dpmsolver++") self.pipe.to("cuda") self.pipe.enable_vae_slicing() self.pipe.enable_model_cpu_offload() self.depth = MidasDetector.from_pretrained("lllyasviel/Annotators") self.loaded_loras = set() def load_lora(self, path: str, name: str): if name not in self.loaded_loras: self.pipe.load_lora_weights(path, adapter_name=name) self.loaded_loras.add(name) def generate(self, spec: GenerationSpec) -> tuple[Image.Image, dict]: if spec.lora_weights: names = list(spec.lora_weights) self.pipe.set_adapters(names, adapter_weights=list(spec.lora_weights.values())) control_image = None if spec.reference_image: ref = Image.open(spec.reference_image).convert("RGB").resize( (spec.width, spec.height)) control_image = self.depth(ref) seed = spec.seed if spec.seed is not None else torch.seed() % 2**32 generator = torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(seed) kwargs = dict( prompt=spec.prompt, negative_prompt=spec.negative_prompt, num_inference_steps=spec.steps, guidance_scale=spec.guidance, width=spec.width, height=spec.height, generator=generator, ) if control_image is not None: kwargs.update(image=control_image, controlnet_conditioning_scale=spec.control_scale, control_guidance_end=spec.control_end) image = self.pipe(**kwargs).images[0] metadata = { "seed": seed, "steps": spec.steps, "guidance": spec.guidance, "control_scale": spec.control_scale if control_image else None, "loras": spec.lora_weights, "prompt": spec.prompt, "scheduler": "DPM++ 2M Karras", } return image, metadata ``` **Return the metadata with every image.** Seed, sampler, scales, and LoRA weights are what make a good result reproducible — and in a catalogue pipeline you *will* need to regenerate image 87 with one small change three weeks later. **`madebyollin/sdxl-vae-fp16-fix`** is worth knowing about: SDXL's default VAE has numerical issues in fp16 producing black or artefact-heavy images. This drop-in replacement fixes it and is standard practice. ##### Evaluating controllable generation ```python import numpy as np import torch from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor class GenerationEvaluator: """Prompt adherence, subject fidelity, and structural conformance.""" def __init__(self, device="cuda"): self.clip = CLIPModel.from_pretrained( "openai/clip-vit-large-patch14").to(device) self.proc = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-large-patch14") self.device = device def clip_score(self, image, prompt: str) -> float: """Text-image alignment. Higher = better prompt adherence.""" inputs = self.proc(text=[prompt], images=image, return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True).to(self.device) with torch.no_grad(): out = self.clip(**inputs) return float(out.logits_per_image[0, 0]) / 100.0 def subject_similarity(self, generated, reference_images: list) -> float: """DINO-style identity check: does it show the RIGHT chair?""" gen_emb = self._image_embedding(generated) ref_embs = [self._image_embedding(r) for r in reference_images] sims = [float(gen_emb @ r) for r in ref_embs] return float(np.mean(sims)) def structure_conformance(self, generated, control_image, detector) -> float: """Does the output match the conditioning structure?""" regenerated = detector(generated) a = np.asarray(regenerated.convert("L"), dtype=np.float32) / 255.0 b = np.asarray(control_image.convert("L"), dtype=np.float32) / 255.0 return float(1.0 - np.abs(a - b).mean()) def _image_embedding(self, image): inputs = self.proc(images=image, return_tensors="pt").to(self.device) with torch.no_grad(): emb = self.clip.get_image_features(**inputs)[0] return (emb / emb.norm()).cpu().numpy() ``` **Three metrics because there are three failure modes.** A generation can follow the prompt but show the wrong chair (low subject similarity), show the right chair in the wrong pose (low structure conformance), or match both while ignoring the styling instruction (low CLIP score). **Human evaluation remains necessary** for aesthetic quality. These metrics catch objective failures; they do not tell you whether the image is good. ##### Common mistakes - **Prompting alone for subject consistency** — two weeks of the wrong chair. - **No prior preservation in DreamBooth**, so every chair becomes your chair. - **Uniform backgrounds in training images**, baking the background into the LoRA. - **`control_guidance_end=1.0`**, over-constraining texture and lighting. - **Combined ControlNet scales above 1.2**, producing rigid artefact-heavy output. - **A real word as the DreamBooth trigger token.** - **Default SDXL VAE in fp16** — use the fp16-fix variant. - **Ancestral samplers in a reproducible pipeline.** - **50 steps with a modern sampler**, where 25–30 is indistinguishable. - **Not saving generation metadata**, making results irreproducible. - **Multiple LoRAs all at weight 1.0**, causing conflict. - **Too many DreamBooth steps** — check intermediate checkpoints rather than assuming the last is best. ##### Hands-on: control the composition Your practical task uses ControlNet conditioned on a pose or edge map and compares samplers. Generate the same prompt with the same seed at `controlnet_conditioning_scale` of 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, and 1.3, and view them together — the progression from suggestion to rigid constraint is immediately visible, and it will set your default. Then sweep `control_guidance_end` and note how releasing the condition late improves surface detail. The mini project trains a style or subject LoRA and builds a controllable pipeline around it. **Vary the backgrounds in your training images** and use prior preservation for a subject LoRA. Save checkpoints at 50%, 75%, and 100% of your step budget and compare them on a prompt the subject should *not* dominate — that comparison is how you find the overfitting point. The assignment writes a guide on controllable diffusion covering ControlNet, LoRA, and IP-Adapter with example use cases. Build the decision table for "what do I need controlled" → "which technique", and be specific about combinations: LoRA for the subject plus ControlNet for the composition is the pairing that solves the catalogue problem, and explaining why each alone is insufficient is the substance of the guide. ##### Key takeaways - **Prompting gives variety; ControlNet and LoRA give control** — and production pipelines need control, not variety. - **ControlNet's zero-initialised convolutions** mean training starts as the unmodified model, exactly like LoRA's zero-initialised B matrix. - **Release the ControlNet condition around 0.8** so composition stays locked while the model refines texture and lighting freely. - **DreamBooth needs prior preservation and varied backgrounds**, 15–30 images, a rare trigger token, and checkpoint comparison to find the overfitting point. - **Try IP-Adapter before training anything** — it costs nothing, and it is often sufficient for style transfer where only a LoRA can deliver true subject fidelity.
practical_task_reference: Use ControlNet to generate images conditioned on a pose or edge map and compare samplers for quality/speed.
